 400 buildings, helipad in Badrinath at risk from potential glacier avalanche: Study 
 Trending Bombay High Court Bengaluru Robbery Delhi Rain Mumbai Siblings Death UP government jobs Kochi Accident Bombay High Court Bengaluru Robbery Delhi Rain Mumbai Siblings Death UP government jobs Kochi Accident Bombay High Court Bengaluru Robbery Delhi Rain Mumbai Siblings Death UP government jobs Kochi Accident 400 buildings, helipad in Badrinath at risk from potential glacier avalanche: Study 
 Gaurav Talwar / Oct 29, 2026, 22:41 IST Save Comments Share Aa + Text Size Small
 Medium
 Large
 Print A satellite image showing three hanging-glacier sites above Badrinath town, with arrows indicating potential avalanche paths towards the valley. The inset photographs show the pilgrimage town situated along the Alaknanda river. Photo credit: Research study Dehradun: Nearly 400 buildings, a helipad, parking areas and 2.66km of transport infrastructure in Badrinath could be affected by an avalanche from a hanging glacier overlooking the Himalayan pilgrimage town in Chamoli district, an international study published on Wednesday warned. Researchers identified one of three glaciers examined as particularly hazardous because of its large ice volume, steep slopes and downstream terrain. However, they clarified that the findings did not suggest an imminent glacier collapse. The study, published in international journal Landslides, estimated that a high-mobility avalanche could affect 398 buildings, 3.87 hectares of agricultural land and 15.57 hectares of forest cover, besides transport infrastructure and other facilities. Titled “Vulnerability assessment of hanging-glacier avalanches in Badrinath Township, Central Himalayas, India”, the research was conducted by scientists from Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru; Defence Geoinformatics Research Establishment (DGRE) under Defence Research and Development Organisation ( DRDO ); and University of Cambridge, UK. Among the three glaciers studied, researchers identified Site 2 as posing the greatest potential threat. They estimated that it could release 5.89 million cubic metres of ice. Its surface slope of 34.57° and bed slope of 30.64°, combined with the terrain below, increased the potential exposure of Badrinath in the simulated scenarios. Hanging glaciers are masses of ice on steep mountain slopes. Sections can break away and descend rapidly into valleys, threatening settlements, roads and other infrastructure along their paths. Researchers used remote-sensing data to identify potential ice-release areas and estimate their volumes. They then modelled avalanche movement using the Rapid Mass Movement Simulation (RAMMS) model under low-, medium- and high-mobility conditions by varying friction parameters. The simulations showed that avalanche speed, flow height and impact pressure changed relatively little even under conditions favouring faster movement and longer travel distances. Differences across the three sites were generally below 7%, suggesting that dangerous avalanches could occur even under less extreme conditions. The study also found that the distance an avalanche travelled did not depend solely on the volume of ice released. The shape of downstream channels and surrounding terrain could allow smaller ice masses to travel considerable distances. The findings highlighted potential risks to Badrinath, a major Char Dham pilgrimage destination, where roads, parking facilities and other infrastructure could fall within avalanche paths under certain conditions. Researchers called for detailed site-specific hazard assessments, early-warning systems, improved land-use planning and greater public awareness to reduce the risks. Referring to the flash floods and rock-ice avalanches that struck northern Nepal in Aug, one of the study’s authors said, “The recent glacier-related disaster in Nepal highlights the risks of mountain instability and its downstream consequences. While the Nepal event and our Badrinath study may involve different failure mechanisms, both underline the need for scientific risk assessments, better monitoring, early-warning preparedness and measures to protect vulnerable communities. ” The researchers emphasised that their findings were based on simulated avalanche scenarios and exposure assessments. They did not establish that a glacier collapse was imminent or that the identified buildings and infrastructure would necessarily suffer damage.
